pages.title: Auditorium Building
pages.text:
The Auditorium Building is a mixed-use early skyscraper at 430 South Michigan Avenue in the Loop community area of Chicago, Illinois, United States. Built between 1887 and 1889, it was designed by Adler & Sullivan, the partnership of Louis Sullivan and Dankmar Adler. The building occupies the northern side of Ida B. Wells Drive between Michigan and Wabash avenues. It originally included the Auditorium Theatre, offices, and a hotel; the theater still exists, but the rest of the building has since been converted into classrooms for Roosevelt University. The building is a  Chicago Landmark and a National Historic Landmark, and it is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
Following the success of the 1885 Grand Opera Festival, Chicago businessman Ferdinand Peck formed a syndicate to develop a theater, office, and hotel building. The building was dedicated on December 9, 1889, and the hotel opened the next year. Originally, the Chicago Auditorium Association (CAA) owned the building, and ownership the land was split three ways. The CAA began looking to replace the building as early as 1922; it subsequently went bankrupt, and the landowners took over in 1932. The building was renovated but was closed in 1941. It was briefly used as a servicemen's center during World War II before being taken over by Roosevelt University in 1946. The university converted the former offices and hotel into classrooms, and the theater inside was renovated between 1958 and 1967. The building has undergone additional modifications throughout the years, including renovations in the early 2000s.
The building is generally 10 stories high, except for a 17-story, 240-foot-tall (73 m) tower to the south. The facade is generally made of darker granite and lighter limestone and is divided into three horizontal sections. Its structural design includes a foundation of grillages and pyramidal footings, along with an iron and steel superstructure. Inside, the theater occupies 40% of the building's volume, with 4,200 seats spread across three seating levels. Surrounding the theater is classroom space formerly used by the hotel to the east and the offices to the west.


== Site ==
The Auditorium Building is located at 430 South Michigan Avenue in the Loop community area of Chicago, Illinois, United States. It occupies a land lot covering 63,500 square feet (5,900 m2) on the southern section of its city block. The block is bounded by Van Buren Street to the north, Wabash Avenue to the west, Ida B. Wells Drive (formerly Congress Parkway) to the south, and Michigan Avenue to the east.
The building has a frontage of about 160 feet (49 m) on Wabash, 360 feet (110 m) on Ida B. Wells, and 187 feet (57 m) on Michigan. On the same block to the north are the Fine Arts Building and the Buckingham Building on Michigan Avenue. Grant Park is to the east across Michigan Avenue, and the Congress Plaza Hotel is to the south across Ida B. Wells Drive. An alley just north of the Auditorium Building is known as Song Bird Alley or Peacock Alley.


== History ==


=== Development ===


==== Origin and purpose ====
Chicago's remaining theaters after the 1871 fire either were small, were inconveniently located, or had poor acoustics. Chicago businessman Ferdinand Peck helped finance construction of Chicago's Central Music Hall, which opened in 1879 and was designed by Dankmar Adler. Shortly afterward, Adler hired Louis Sullivan, who eventually became a partner in their architectural practice, Adler & Sullivan. As a direct result of the Music Hall commission, they were hired to design several auditoriums across the midwestern US. These included a temporary theater for the Grand Opera Festival in Chicago, hosted by the Opera Festival Association, an organization formed by Peck. The Opera Festival ran for two weeks in April 1885, attracting up to 115,000 attendees. The success of the Opera Festival prompted Peck to build a permanent opera house in Chicago.  
At the Opera Festival Association's annual meeting in May 1885, the group created a committee to obtain land for a new theater building. Peck sought a site on Michigan Avenue's west sidewalk, and to save money, he initially considered developing on a publicly owned site. To offset the theater's operating losses, Peck proposed constructing hotel rooms around it, catering to the area's high demand for hospitality. Historian Joseph Siry writes that the early plans did not mention offices, of which relatively few had been developed along downtown Chicago's eastern edge.
By late 1885, Peck had proposed a public–private partnership with the Chicago Public Library to develop a combination theater–library at Michigan Avenue and Randolph Street. After receiving pushback, Peck dropped his suggestion in favor of a fully privately funded theater. Another site fronting Lake Michigan was dismissed, and Peck also reportedly considered sites on Michigan Avenue at Congress or Monroe streets. By January 1886, the Peck syndicate contemplated obtaining the northwest corner of Michigan Avenue and Congress Street, where six owners possessed 11 land lots. Peck's friend Wirt D. Walker bought an option for the lots, extending west to Wabash Avenue, from the Scammon estate that March. After obtaining full ownership, Walker gave Peck a sixty-day option on the land that June. Walker did not yet own the block's southwestern corner, which was occupied by the Brunswick Hotel and some houses. The city government had also set aside part of the block for a future north–south alley, though this land was later given to Peck's syndicate.


==== Incorporation, funding, and design ====
After acquiring the land, Peck immediately announced plans for a hotel, office, and theater building. Illinois law at the time forbade the creation of corporations solely for real estate development. Accordingly, Peck and his partners incorporated the Chicago Grand Auditorium Association (CGAA) that July to both develop the building and operate the theater. By then, Walker, the Peck family, and Studebaker Bros. had consolidated ownership of the site, which had been merged into five lots. Adler & Sullivan had drawn their first known plan for the site by August 1886, although they had not been hired yet. Sullivan's first design, published the next month, called for a Romanesque structure with a brick, stone, and terracotta facade, along with a central tower and a high pitched roof. The ornate facade was intended to draw the attention of passengers riding trains along the nearby waterfront.
Meanwhile, the CGAA sold $2 million of stock and issued $900,000 in bonds. The stock sales funded only construction, not any of the theater's operating expenses, and stockholders were not given any incentives such as box seats. An initial tranche of stock worth $750,000 was issued in November 1886 at $100 per share. Early shareholders included Marshall Field, the Chicago City Railway, Martin A. Ryerson, Charles L. Hutchinson, and N. K. Fairbank, along with Adler & Sullivan and Peck. The CGAA selected a board of directors on December 4; before the board's first meeting the next week, Sullivan sent the stockholders revised plans. By then, Peck envisioned a 5,000-seat theater with a massive stage, two gallery levels, and 51 boxes. Following agitation among directors who opposed Adler & Sullivan's appointment, Sullivan drew up a compromise plan, which called for a 10-story, flat-roofed structure with a pyramidal-roofed tower. Peck proposed that a third-party expert review Sullivan's plans, inviting Sullivan's former teacher William Ware to examine them.

The CGAA hired Adler & Sullivan on December 22, 1886, before Ware had reviewed the plans. The next month, the corporation increased its capital stock to $1.5 million and renamed itself the Chicago Auditorium Association (CAA). Adler & Sullivan draftsman Paul Mueller said that, by then, Sullivan had devised drawings for an elaborate terracotta building with bay windows and second-story columns. Ware visited Chicago on January 17, 1887, and suggested minor changes to the exterior, particularly to the tower and the facade's horizontal subdivisions. Following Ware's visit, the CAA's directors directed Adler & Sullivan to complete exterior drawings on January 29. The corporation signed 99-year leases for the site, finalizing agreements with the landowners in January and February. Fifteen draftsmen spent half a year devising the detailed drawings. The design was repeatedly revised during early 1887, much to Adler's dismay; on several occasions, draftsmen completed drawings only to find that the CAA's needs had changed yet again. Frank Lloyd Wright, who joined Adler & Sullivan that year, helped work on the design. 


==== Construction ====
The CAA began soliciting bids for the foundation on January 17, the day Ware visited, and work had begun by the end of the month. Most of the site was cleared the first week of February, and later that month William Sooy Smith conducted test borings to ascertain how much weight the ground could carry. Two hundred workers and thirty horse teams worked continuously on foundations, demolishing the existing buildings while foundation work proceeded concurrently on other, already-cleared parts of the site. In the meantime, the CAA awarded dozens of contracts for the project; this contrasted with newer buildings where work was handled by a single general contractor. The Brunswick Hotel was demolished after its lease expired on May 1, and the CAA's directors voted on May 6 to use limestone, rather than brick and terracotta, above the second floor. Later that month, the foundation was completed, and the CAA and architects agreed to use rose-tinted Minnesota gray granite for the lower facade. A construction permit for the superstructure was issued on June 25, and foundation work was finished that July. 

Workers used temporary falsework to support steel and iron girders until the permanent walls and columns were completed. Because of the project's high rate of accidents, contractors took out life insurance policies and distributed disability benefits to injured workers. Adler also modified the theater's design to accommodate a theatrical organ. Peck invited US President Grover Cleveland to lay the building's cornerstone; this drew complaints from labor unions, as Cleveland was not a union worker, and he ultimately refused to lay the cornerstone. Instead Cleveland visited the site on October 5, 1887, and the cornerstone was laid the next day. Concurrently, Chicago businesspeople wanted the city to host the Democratic National Convention (DNC) and Republican National Convention (RNC) in 1888, even as labor unions encouraged the DNC and RNC to boycott the Auditorium Building. While the 1888 DNC was ultimately held in St. Louis, the Auditorium Building was selected for the 1888 RNC in December 1887. Granite cutters went on strike that month after making very little progress on the facade. By then, brickwork and ironwork were being installed, and trusses over the theater were being added. Work on the theater was hastened for the RNC, even as the building around it was delayed. The CAA took over the granite supplier's Minnesota quarry in January 1888. After finding that the quarry could not supply large enough blocks for some columns, Adler & Sullivan ordered granite from Maine. Three-fourths of the iron had been delivered by March, but the steel supplier had difficulty keeping up with demand. The planned tower was also increased to 17 stories mid-construction. The theater was being roofed in by early 1888, and facade work had reached the fifth floor by June. That month, Milward Adams was selected to manage the theater. Temporary lighting and thousands of temporary seats were installed for the RNC, where Benjamin Harrison was nominated as the Republican presidential candidate. 
The CAA hired Frank Roosevelt in August 1888 to produce the theater's organ. Construction of the offices was accelerated, as the CAA wished to begin renting out offices in May 1889. Additional contracts, such as those for plasterwork and ornamentation, were awarded through 1888 and 1889. By December 1888, the shareholders had rented out some of the offices, and interior finishes were being installed. By then, rising costs prompted the CAA to issue additional bonds. Shortly thereafter, while digging the theater's stage pit, workers began to detect settlement under the building.   


==== Completion and opening ====
With work nearing completion, the CAA began looking for a hotel operator in October 1888; given the low expected annual income of $50,000, they had difficulty convincing a local hotelier to operate the hotel. J. H. Breslin and R. H. Southgate, who respectively operated the Gilsey House and the Brunswick Hotel in New York, agreed to operate it in early 1889. A new entity, the Auditorium Hotel Company, was incorporated. Breslin and Southgate wanted the hotel to also include a banquet hall, which Adler hastily added to the seventh floor above the theater. Breslin and Southgate originally owned five-sixths of the hotel, but Charles W. Shepard, who owned the remaining one-sixth, sold them his ownership stake that August. The tower's masonry was finished in June 1889, and a capstone dedication ceremony was held that October 2. Just before the building's formal opening that December, the CAA increased its capital stock to $2 million. 
The Auditorium Building was dedicated on December 9, 1889, with an audience of 5,000 inside and 10,000 outside. President Harrison dedicated the building and opera star Adelina Patti sang "Home Sweet Home". The theater's first performance, Gounod's Roméo et Juliette, was staged the next night. The hotel was still under construction; due to delays completing the finishes, the hotel's dining room was not used until January 1890. The hotel officially opened on March 15, and the banquet hall opened that October. In total, the building had cost over $3 million. For their work, Adler & Sullivan earned $75,000 in cash and stock—representing a 2.5% commission, which barely covered their expenses. Adler & Sullivan were also offered some office space at reduced rental rates.


=== Early years ===
For its first several decades, the building hosted various events and political conventions. The 400-room Auditorium Hotel was larger than many of its nearby competitors. The hotel hosted several US presidents, along with several Republican Party candidates' presidential campaigns. The theater hosted opera singers such as Enrico Caruso, Amelita Galli-Curci, Mary Garden, John McCormack, Nellie Melba, and Ellen Terry, presenting up to 38 operas per year. It was also used for ballet, orchestra, and concerts. The CAA was less profitable: It only ever issued one dividend to stockholders over the years.  


==== 1890s to 1910s ====

In July 1891, the CAA extended its land leases by 100 years. At the time, Henry J. Willing owned most of the land; Francis Bartlett and William A. Slater owned the southwest corner, while Studebaker owned the northeast corner. The building's walls had settled 6 inches (150 mm) by then. The Chicago Symphony Orchestra began performing at the theater that October, and Adler & Sullivan also opened their office on the tower's top floors; by then, the offices were 75% occupied. The hotel was less profitable, in part because the guestrooms lacked en-suite bathrooms, a feature common in newer hotels. The CAA issued another $1.6 million of bonds in 1892 to fund the building's continued operation. After William Fitzgerald proposed erecting another hotel across Congress Street in 1892, the CAA bought Fitzgerald's land to avert prospective competition. The CAA developed the Auditorium Annex (later Congress Hotel) there the next year, constructing an adjacent power plant that served both the original building and the annex. This freed up additional basement space for rental purposes.
The Auditorium Hotel and Annex accommodated large numbers of guests during the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, after which the CAA's directors issued their dividend. By the late 1890s, the theater's walls had been repainted, as they contrasted with the colors of female patrons' gowns. The Auditorium Building also became unprofitable after the exposition, prompting Peck's resignation from the board of directors in 1900. The building's outer walls had continued to settle, and that year Adler asked Mueller about whether the interior columns could be shortened to even out the floor levels. This was never carried out, as Adler died that year. For fire safety, fire escapes were added in 1901, and firewalls were added after the Iroquois Theatre fire two years later. In part because of the Auditorium's inadequate facilities, the Symphony Orchestra relocated to Orchestra Hall in 1904. Although the theater continued hosting traveling acts and political speeches, the building was losing convention business to the significantly larger Chicago Coliseum.
In 1906, Sullivan drew up plans to replace the theater with more hotel rooms, expanding the Auditorium Building to 20 or 22 stories, but nothing came of this proposal. The CAA took over the hotel's operation from the previous owners in March 1909, following the expiry of the previous lease. Subsequently, Benjamin Marshall renovated the hotel's Michigan Avenue guestrooms and basement in 1910 and drew up plans for ground-floor renovations, which were not carried out. That year, after the Chicago Grand Opera Company became the Auditorium Theatre's resident opera company, Marshall renovated the theater, adding boxes and raising the stage floor. Despite the hotel and theater renovations, the building's financials remained stagnant; any savings were counteracted by depreciation and sharply increased property taxes. The scale of the losses was not made evident until 1918, when the CAA's balance sheets began recording depreciation charges.


==== 1920s and 1930s ====
The Auditorium Hotel opened its first store, an apparel shop, in 1922. By the following year, the CAA planned to demolish and replace the Auditorium Building, citing its continued unprofitability. As the terms of the existing ground leases forbade demolition, the CAA sued the landowners in February 1923 to change the lease terms, but Peck and the landowners opposed demolition. The CAA claimed the building was about to collapse, in an unsuccessful attempt to have courts rule in their favor. A judicial decision was deferred for several years, and the US Supreme Court ultimately declined to hear the case in October 1928. The demolition plans were thus abandoned. That year, a syndicate of Chicago businessmen took a controlling interest in the CAA.
The Grand Opera Company moved to the Civic Opera House in 1929, performing its final show at the Auditorium Theatre that January. One of the CAA's bond issues matured the next month, but the association was unable to pay the face value of $834,000 to bondholders. The Auditorium Theatre subsequently closed, and the CAA declared bankruptcy. The CAA's receiver proposed converting the theater to a miniature golf course. The receiver attempted to convince the building's shareholders to move their shares in a common fund, but although most shareholders agreed to do so, this did not raise sufficient money for the organization. The four landowners—Northwestern Mutual and the Willing, Sears, and Slater estates—solicited bids for the building's demolition in 1930 and 1931. The lowest demolition bid was submitted for $400,000, more than the land valuation.
In 1932, the landowners took ownership of the building and created a syndicate, the Auditorium Building Corporation, to manage it. John Goodridge of the Willing estate led the syndicate. Northwestern Mutual declined to join, requiring the remaining landowners to seek the company's permission for any modifications under its section of land. The owners hired Holabird & Root to conduct renovations. The firm repaired the tower's foundations and the theater's ceiling trusses, and it redecorated the hotel to accommodate visitors to the Century of Progress world's fair. The theater renovation cost $125,000 and involved the installation of new boxes and an entrance canopy, replacement of lighting, repainting, and removal of an art-glass skylight. The theater reopened in December 1932, but its success was short-lived. By the late 1930s, the building had a net annual income of only $35,000, while the property taxes alone were double that amount. Nonetheless, Holabird & Root deemed the building itself structurally sound, and the theater was still hosting events.


==== 1940s: Closure and servicemen's center ====

The Auditorium Building Corporation had accumulated $1.15 million in debt by 1940 and was severely delinquent on its property taxes. The corporation announced in May 1941 that the building would close the next month, after the nearby Congress Hotel decided to stop providing heat, power, and water to the Auditorium; the corporation lacked money to pay for its own utility plant. In response, local civic groups convened to appoint a committee to advocate for city takeover of the building, and Mayor Edward Joseph Kelly chartered the Auditorium Music Foundation to convert it into a music center. After a 30-day extension of utility service, the Auditorium Building was shuttered entirely on July 31, 1941. All tenants moved away except for a few store owners.
The Auditorium Music Foundation sought to raise $400,000 to convert the theater into a performance venue. The group wanted to reopen the theater by November 1941, but it had raised only $250,000 within a year. The Cook County government filed a foreclosure suit against the building in June 1942, intending to auction off the decorations and furnishings. The county had wanted to auction the entire building, but Northwestern Mutual had paid the back taxes for its own site, preventing such an auction. The county government approved takeover of the building later that month, and the furnishings were sold as scheduled. The city government obtained ownership of the other lots, taking over the structure in July. Excluded from this acquisition was a 52-by-170-foot (16 by 52 m) parcel at the building's northeast corner, covering parts of the theater and half the hotel.
The building became a World War II servicemen's center, occupying the first two stories. A bowling alley was added inside the theater, a lunch counter replaced the original bar, and the decorations were painted over. A temporary boiler plant was added as well, and a music room was built on the fourth floor in 1943. The northeast corner parcel was sold in 1945 to attorney Abraham Teitelbaum. Teitelbaum proposed buying the building early the next year. Kelly also proposed that the building be permanently retained as a recreation center, but ultimately the servicemen's center operated for only a short period over the war. The center closed in May 1946 after accommodating ten million soldiers.


=== Roosevelt University ownership ===


==== Mid-1940s and 1950s ====
 Roosevelt University bought most of the building in August 1946, paying the Willing, Sears, and Slater estates $400,000. In exchange, the university assumed $1.3 million in back taxes. The university took over the next month and renovated the former hotel space over the next several months. The Auditorium Theater Foundation repaid its creditors and dissolved that year; the theater stood vacant for another two decades and was used for storage. Ownership was still split with Teitelbaum, requiring each owner to gain the other's consent to use parts of the building. Some elements, such as the theater curtain, a heating plant, and elevator machinery, straddled both sections. Teitelbaum initially wanted $2 million, a price the college found exorbitant; he then erected chicken-wire fence between the two portions of the building. He ultimately sold his land to the college in February 1947 for $402,000, and students began using the Auditorium Building that year. The former hotel's lobby, lounge, and dining room respectively became the university's lobby, lounge, and library.
In 1950, the city government announced plans to widen the neighboring section of Congress Street into Congress Parkway. Roosevelt University contemplated converting the theater into a production studio around that time. As part of the Congress widening project, Roosevelt University agreed to cede a section of the first floor to the city in 1952, in exchange for having all back taxes waived. Some ground-floor rooms and part of the theater lobby were removed to make way for a sidewalk arcade; the Chicago Daily Tribune called these demolitions "a great pity". The arcade, built by Walsh Brothers for $337,999, was completed in 1956. During the decade, as the building's stained-glass windows fell into disrepair, they were replaced with clear panes. The 17-story office tower had been closed off because of structural deterioration, and the university unsuccessfully sought an external organization to restore the theater. Wright, who supported the building's preservation, called the theater's dilapidated condition "Chicago's shame and a universal disgrace" and offered to help with renovation. 
The university announced plans in 1955 to convert the banquet hall into Ganz Recital Hall. Interest in Sullivan's architecture was renewed during his 100th birthday in 1956. By then, Roosevelt University was giving twice-weekly tours of the building and was looking to rent out its space, including the theater, for up to $200,000 annually. The university contemplated restoring the theater for the Chicago Symphony Orchestra, commencing tours of the space in late 1956. At the time, few of Chicago's other large theaters remained operational. The university also raised $75,000 to renovate Ganz Recital Hall; architect Crombie Taylor was hired to design Ganz Hall's renovation, which was completed in 1957. The next year, Roosevelt University trustees passed a resolution to restore the exterior, theater, and other major interior spaces to their original appearances, and reuse or modernize other interiors. The trustees also appointed a committee to study a $2.7 million renovation for the theater. Also in 1958, Taylor converted the ladies' parlor into the Louis Sullivan Room, following a $50,000 gift from urban planner Morris Hirsch.


==== 1960s and 1970s: Renovations ====

The Auditorium Theater Council (ATC) was formed in 1960 to oversee the theater's renovation, though Roosevelt University retained ownership of the physical theater. The ATC was allowed to use the theater rent-free but could not borrow money to pay for the project. Beatrice T. Spachner, a Roosevelt University trustee, headed the ATC. Encouraged by then-recent preservation efforts at New York's Carnegie Hall, the ATC hired Taylor and Skidmore, Owings & Merrill (SOM) as design consultants in 1961. SOM claimed the building was structurally unsound and that it would cost $4.25 million to renovate the building. The damage was subsequently deemed to not be severe. Even so, Taylor said that defective drainage caused rainwater to pour onto the stage. Taylor oversaw an additional renovation of the second-floor hotel lounge in 1962. The next year, Roosevelt University contemplated a 20-story annex abutting the Auditorium Building, and the university spent a year remodeling the Wabash Avenue storefronts into a bookstore.  
Harry Weese was hired to restore the theater, having offered to refurbish it at a price much lower than what SOM was offering. Work on the stage was underway by early 1964 after the ATC had raised $762,000 and received a permit to renovate the stage. Fundraising was complicated by competition from the newly completed McCormick Place, which also had a theater. After over $1.7 million had been raised by 1966, work on the theater stalled, prompting an emergency fundraising effort that November. The ATC had raised another half-million dollars by June 1967, bringing its total budget to $2.25 million, enough to reopen the theater. By the next month, Roosevelt University had raised $6.4 million for a separate renovation of the building, which included restoring the office tower and adding interior floor area to the central rooftop courtyard.

On October 31, 1967, the ATC reopened the Auditorium Theatre with a performance of A Midsummer Night's Dream, proceeds from which were used for further renovations. By then, Roosevelt University was renovating the tower and courtyard, and it was adding a mezzanine within one floor of the tower. The building renovations were designed by Gutnayer & Associates, who found that the foundation could support the additional weight. Roosevelt University erected a 17-story dormitory tower next to the building in 1970, while the ATC continued to restore theatrical facilities such as the dressing rooms and stage. In 1972, Roosevelt University completed its renovation for $3.66 million, which included modernization of classrooms, laboratories, and other educational facilities. 
The hotel lobby was renovated in 1973 by Brenner, Danforth and Rockwell, which involved uncovering the mosaic floor and removing an existing partition. That year, the recital hall was renovated into the O'Malley Theater. The state government sought federal funding in 1975 for further restoration of the Auditorium Building, as part of a $1.3 million initiative to upgrade 25 historic Chicago-area buildings. Stained glass windows in the hotel stair and Ganz Hall were restored that year. In 1976, Roosevelt University promised $3.891 million for further renovations and sought a matching funds grant for the other half of that renovation. For their respective renovations, Roosevelt University and Spachner received awards from the National Trust for Historic Preservation in 1978.

pages.title: Adler & Sullivan
pages.text:
Adler & Sullivan was an architectural firm founded by Dankmar Adler and Louis Sullivan in Chicago. Among its projects was the multi-purpose Auditorium Building in Chicago and the Wainwright Building skyscraper in St Louis. In 1883 Louis Sullivan was added to Adler's architectural firm, creating the Adler & Sullivan partnership. According to Architect Ward Miller:

Adler & Sullivan are most associated with being an innovative and progressive architectural practice, forwarding the idea of an American style and expressing this in a truly modern format. Their work was widely published and at the forefront of building construction. Their buildings and especially their multipurpose structures ... were unequaled. Furthermore, the expression of a tall building, its structure with a definite base, middle section or shaft and top or cornice was a new approach for the high building design. These types of tall structures developed into a format.  ... Even today, the vertical expression of a building employs these design principals.
Adler, with his engineering prowess and facility with acoustics became seen as the business genius of the partnership, while Sullivan, known for his great design talent, is recounted as the artist.


== Selected commissions ==
Ann Halsted House, Chicago, Illinois, 1883
Halsted Row Houses, Chicago, Illinois, 1884
Leon Mannheimer House, Chicago, Illinois, 1884
Desenberg Building, Kalamazoo, Michigan, 1885
Joseph Deimel House, Chicago, Illinois, 1886
Auditorium Building, Chicago, Illinois 1889
Pueblo Opera House, Pueblo, Colorado,  1890

Wainwright Building, St. Louis, Missouri,  1891
Charnley-Norwood House, Ocean Springs, Mississippi, 1891
Louis Sullivan Bungalow, Ocean Springs, Mississippi, 1891

Albert Sullivan House, Chicago, Illinois, 1891
Union Trust Building, St. Louis (1893; street-level ornament heavily altered in 1924)
